CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment.

Identity has become a critical attack surface. Adversaries exploit valid credentials to move laterally, escalate privileges, and operate undetected. Human, non-human, and AI agent identities continue to multiply across organizations, both expanding the attack surface and introducing new security challenges. AI agents in particular can autonomously access applications, invoke tools, and take action at machine speed, fundamentally changing how organizations must approach identity security.

Traditional identity security, built around static access decisions and periodic checks, can no longer keep pace. Organizations need continuous visibility into identity risk and the ability to enforce access decisions in real time.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader validates our approach to Continuous Identity, which brings together identity visibility, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. With innovations like the recent CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider, we're extending our approach to secure AI agents with verifiable identities and tightly scoped, just-in-time access.

Identity Security for the Modern Enterprise

CrowdStrike capabilities demonstrate the value of Continuous Identity, from unified visibility and real-time risk intelligence to dynamic enforcement across the enterprise:

Unified endpoint and identity visibility: Identity attacks do not stay in one domain, and neither does our view of them. The CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor sees local and bypass authentication, network telemetry decrypts NTLM and SMB exchanges, and the identity graph updates in real time. By correlating endpoint and identity signals, CrowdStrike helps security teams identify suspicious behavior across the attack path and respond with greater context.

Rapid deployment: The Falcon platform brings identity and endpoint security together through one console and one sensor, which establishes identity visibility and coverage in hours to days. Policy templates, simulation, and audit modes support staged rollouts, which helps organizations operationalize identity security while minimizing disruption.

Real-time identity risk intelligence: CrowdStrike’s unified risk score updates in under a minute, includes blast radius, and feeds every downstream enforcement control with reevaluation after authentication and midsession intervention. These capabilities help security teams understand identity risk in context, prioritize threats, and make enforcement decisions. By connecting identity signals with security context from across the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike helps turn visibility into action.

Enforcement that keeps up with the session: CrowdStrike enforces zero standing privileges with auto-approved just-in-time elevation, bidirectional enforcement, post-authentication risk reevaluation, and mid-session intervention. This is Continuous Identity in practice: Access is continuously evaluated as risk changes, and privileges are adjusted or revoked when conditions warrant.

Standards participation: CrowdStrike leads working groups on CAEP, Shared Signals, RISC, and AuthZEN. These initiatives support interoperability and the exchange of identity risk signals across systems, helping organizations extend continuous identity security throughout their environments.

Together, these capabilities bring Continuous Identity to life, connecting visibility, risk intelligence, and real-time enforcement to help organizations stop identity-driven attacks.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider

CrowdStrike's approach to Continuous Identity goes beyond point-in-time authentication. By unifying identity posture management, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the Falcon platform, organizations can continuously assess identity risk, reduce standing privileges, and dynamically adjust or revoke access as risk changes.

As AI agents operate autonomously across enterprise environments, this approach is even more critical. CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

The Future of Identity is Continuous

Identity security can no longer rely on point-in-time decisions. As human, non-human, and AI agent identities expand, organizations need continuous visibility into risk and the ability to enforce access in real time.

CrowdStrike is redefining identity security by moving beyond traditional approaches:

Static access becomes real-time control.

Fragmented tools become a unified platform.

Implicit trust becomes continuous, risk-based enforcement.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape reinforces our vision for Continuous Identity and our commitment to securing every identity and stopping identity-driven attacks.

November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

Critical RCE Vulnerabilities in Windows Services

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

CVE-2026-112967 is a heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service. An in-network attacker can call arbitrary endpoints on the service to trigger the flaw. Enterprise exposure depends on whether the service is present and running. Consumer-oriented Windows SKUs and gaming-enabled configurations are the primary population, making this lower priority for most corporate fleets.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. The attack path is notable: An unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an Exchange Server, and the search indexer processes the attachment automatically for indexing. The recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation grants code execution with the permissions of the indexing service. Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. The Windows Search path is the more significant exposure for enterprise environments. Email-delivered payloads that trigger without user interaction have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they bypass the phishing-click dependency that slows most initial access campaigns.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

CVE-2026-119958 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows LDAP with a CVSS score of 9.8. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted LDAP calls to a listening server. No authentication or user interaction is required.

LDAP is the directory access protocol that underpins Active Directory. Every domain controller exposes LDAP on TCP/389 (and TCP/636 for LDAPS) by design, and the service cannot be disabled without breaking domain operations. Member servers, workstations, and applications query LDAP continuously for authentication, group policy retrieval, and object lookups, making it one of the most heavily trafficked protocols inside any AD environment.

The scope-of-impact concern is substantial. Code execution within the LDAP service on a domain controller places the attacker inside the trust boundary that every other domain resource relies on. From that position, credential extraction, replication abuse, and lateral movement to additional DCs become straightforward follow-on actions. Because LDAP is network-reachable from any domain-joined host by default, any internal foothold that can route to a DC can attempt exploitation.

Unauthenticated RCE flaws in core AD infrastructure have historically drawn rapid attention from ransomware operators and targeted intrusion actors because they collapse the gap between initial access and domain-wide compromise.

Preview Pane-Triggered RCE Vulnerabilities Across Microsoft Office

Eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities this month share a common attack vector: the Preview Pane in Outlook and Word. All carry CVSS scores of 7.5 to 8.8, with seven of the eight scoring 8.8. The underlying flaw classes are use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (two CVEs), release of invalid pointer (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). Despite the variation in memory-corruption primitives, the exploitation pattern is uniform: An attacker delivers a malicious document or email, and merely selecting it for preview triggers code execution with the user's privileges.

The Outlook vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309) are the highest-exposure items in this group. Email is the delivery mechanism, and the Preview Pane is enabled by default in most enterprise Outlook deployments. An external attacker who can send mail to a target organization can reach the vulnerable code path without any authentication or prior foothold. The Word vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110067, CVE-2026-111285, CVE-2026-124185) require document delivery, which typically means a phishing attachment or a link to a malicious file, but still fire on preview rather than open.

The remaining two CVEs (CVE-2026-111289, CVE-2026-120003) affect the broader Office suite and follow the same preview-triggered pattern. CVE-2026-124185 has a lower score (7.5) due to high attack complexity, but the others require no special conditions beyond user receipt of the malicious content.

Preview Pane vulnerabilities have historically been attractive to phishing operators and initial-access brokers because delivery converts directly to execution, with no need to persuade a user to open an attachment.

Critical Vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)

CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 are Critical vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services that both stem from incorrect authorization flaws. The two CVEs share a flaw class but differ in outcome and attack complexity.

CVE-2026-118146 carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and enables RCE. An authenticated attacker with low-level access to an affected server can send a specially crafted request and execute code without any user interaction. The authorization flaw means the server fails to properly validate that the authenticated principal should be permitted to perform the requested operation, turning a low-privilege foothold into code execution on a domain controller.

CVE-2026-118148 has a CVSS score of 7.5 and results in elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. This vulnerability has high attack complexity because successful exploitation requires the attacker to win a race condition. An authenticated attacker who can trigger the race gains SYSTEM privileges on the domain controller.

Active Directory Domain Services provides directory and authentication services for Windows enterprise domains. Domain controllers running AD DS issue Kerberos tickets, store the directory database, and process authentication and authorization decisions for every domain-joined resource. Compromise of a domain controller typically means compromise of the entire domain, since the attacker gains access to credential material and can issue arbitrary authentication assertions.

The attack surface for both vulnerabilities is any domain controller reachable from an authenticated low-privileged foothold. In most enterprise deployments, that includes every writable DC in the forest. Incorrect authorization flaws in identity platform components have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they convert commodity initial access into domain-wide compromise without requiring credential theft or additional tooling.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server

CVE-2026-118207 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server with a CVSS score of 8.8. The flaw stems from use of an incorrectly resolved name or reference, allowing an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send a specially crafted request and execute code on the server. No user interaction is required.

Microsoft Exchange Server provides enterprise email, calendar, and collaboration services, and is commonly deployed with internet-facing client access services for mobile and web users. The authentication requirement lowers the bar only modestly in most environments: Any compromised mailbox credential, service account, or partner federation relationship satisfies it. Once that requirement is met, the attacker reaches code execution on a server that typically holds sensitive mail content, internal address lists, and often enjoys elevated trust relationships with Active Directory.

Organizations running on-premises Exchange frequently expose Outlook Web Access, Exchange ActiveSync, and Autodiscover endpoints to the internet. Servers in this posture are reachable from any network position once the attacker obtains valid credentials, and successful exploitation yields a foothold inside the perimeter on infrastructure that processes sensitive communications.

Exchange Server vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attention from nation-state threat actors and ransomware operators because the combination of internet exposure, high-value data, and domain trust relationships makes compromised Exchange servers effective pivot points for broader intrusions.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V

Microsoft addresses eight Critical elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V this month, spanning five distinct flaw classes: use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (one CVE), TOCTOU race condition (one CVE), untrusted pointer dereference (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). CVSS scores range from 6.4 to 8.2, with CVE-2026-113753 at the top of the range.

The exploitation outcomes fall into two categories. CVE-2026-113753 allows an attacker to gain Virtual Trust Level 1 (VTL1) privileges, which means escaping from the normal kernel (VTL0) into the secure kernel layer that underpins Virtualization-Based Security features such as Credential Guard. Five of the remaining seven CVEs enable guest-to-host escape: An attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine can execute code on the host in the security context of the virtual machine worker process.

Hyper-V is the hypervisor layer that runs Azure compute infrastructure and powers client-side Windows features including Windows Sandbox, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, and Virtualization-Based Security. The exposure therefore reaches both datacenter server populations and ordinary endpoints where these features are enabled.

Most of the cluster carries a high attack complexity because exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk. Hypervisor escapes of this class have historically attracted attention from advanced adversaries because a successful exploit compromises the isolation boundary that separates tenants in shared infrastructure and protects credential material on endpoints.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Services

CVE-2026-119957 is a Critical elevation of privilege vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Services with a CVSS score of 7.8. The flaw is a double-free that requires the attacker to win a race condition. Although exploitation is local, successful exploitation allows an attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine to escape to the host and gain the privileges of the affected virtualization service.

Remote Desktop Services underpins RDP-based remote administration across Windows Server deployments and is a core component in Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environments. The guest-to-host escape path described in Microsoft's FAQ elevates this from a local privilege escalation to a potential hypervisor boundary violation, which matters in any multi-tenant or shared-host scenario.

The attack complexity is high due to the race condition. Post-compromise scenarios where an attacker already controls a guest VM provide the dwell time needed to attempt exploitation repeatedly. RDS-based session hosts and VDI pools present the most exposure to this guest-to-host escalation path.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows SMB Server

CVE-2026-113825 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in the Windows SMB Server Network Transport Driver (srvnet.sys) with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a race condition that an authenticated attacker can trigger over the network to execute code. Microsoft notes that successful exploitation requires the attacker to win the race, which accounts for the high attack-complexity rating.

SMB is the native file-sharing protocol for Windows and is enabled by default on both client and server editions. The srvnet.sys driver handles the network transport layer for SMB traffic, sitting beneath the higher-level SMB2 and SMB3 protocol handlers. SMB listens on TCP/445 and is fundamental to domain operations such as SYSVOL replication, Group Policy delivery, and administrative shares.

The authentication requirement limits drive-by exploitation from the internet, but any attacker who has already obtained low-privileged domain credentials, or who operates from a compromised workstation, can attempt the race. Timing-based flaws in kernel-mode network drivers can be unreliable on a single attempt, yet become practical when an attacker can retry at scale across many hosts. Ransomware operators and targeted intrusion operators have historically exploited race-condition RCE flaws in legacy network services for lateral movement and wormable propagation.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler

CVE-2026-113752 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a use-after-free that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger over an adjacent network. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk in contested LAN environments.

Windows Print Spooler manages print job queuing and driver loading on Windows endpoints and servers. It runs with SYSTEM privileges by default and is enabled on virtually every Windows installation, including workstations that have no physical printer attached. The adjacent-network attack vector limits exposure to attackers who already have a foothold on the same network segment, but that constraint is often satisfied during post-compromise lateral movement.

Print Spooler vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attacker attention because the service combines broad default deployment, high privilege, and a complex legacy codebase that has repeatedly yielded exploitable flaws.

Context: Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy...
Full Text:
Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

When individual signals are brought together, a clear picture forms. With Dynamic Risk Scoring (Q4), agent risk feeds into the same 0 to 100 risk score that Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already builds for the agent's owner and host. When an agent, its user, and its device all climb the risk list together, the coordination behind otherwise routine activity is harder to miss.

This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on. AI Ecosystem Detections (Q4) add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and the compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. When the threat starts in a trusted tool rather than the agent itself, the Falcon platform is watching there too.

Because the context around an agent doesn't always live inside the Falcon platform, Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data where it already lives, without re-ingestion. New connectors for GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake are now generally available, with Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4.

Act on Tough Questions

Once a risky agent surfaces, every analyst faces the same question: Did an agent’s owner do this, or did their agent do it without them knowing?

This is the work Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) was built for. SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working the case together on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity.

Investigation coverage already spans the full range of Falcon platform and third-party sources. In Q4, triage coverage extends to CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian, CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security, CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield, CrowdStrike Falcon® Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. When an agent is flagged, it routes straight into an agentic investigation where the agent, its owner, and its host are already connected.

This shared context is what answers the tough question. Investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate it from what the agent did on its own. When the person's request was routine and everything that followed traces to instructions they never wrote, the verdict becomes clear: The insider was the agent, not the employee.

But a verdict doesn't stop a compromised agent that's still running. The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) is where response happens. Teams build, run, and govern all automation in the SOC, from AI agents to workflows to custom apps, in plain language. They set the mission and define triggers, data, rules, and actions to decide what runs autonomously and what requires approval. A single response decision can coordinate everything that needs to follow in parallel: stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. It's open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP, so teams can govern automation across the security stack with visibility into what it's costing and what needs attention.

See it in action:

Autonomy That Earns Its Trust

As SOCs hand more of the work to agents, the controls that keep agents accountable matter as much as the speed they deliver.

CrowdStrike builds governance into every layer of the agentic SOC. It starts by watching the SOC's agents. Policy-Drift Agent Guardrails, powered by Falcon Guardian (Beta, Q4), screen every CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ and AgentWorks interaction for policy drift, unauthorized tool calls, and out-of-bounds data access to catch the moment an agent steps outside its intended scope.

Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.

The CrowdStrike Advantage in AI-Powered Red Teaming

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines three core CrowdStrike capabilities to bring real-world adversary behavior into AI-powered red team testing:

Industry-leading adversary intelligence: CrowdStrike pioneered adversary-driven threat intelligence and tracks more than 290 adversaries globally. Recognized as a Leader by both Gartner and Forrester in threat intelligence, CrowdStrike draws on frontline threat hunting, incident response, CrowdStrike Falcon® platform telemetry, and intelligence on emerging threats to bring the latest adversary tradecraft directly into red team testing.

Deep knowledge of customer environments: The Falcon platform provides rich context across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, configurations, and security controls. This enables CrowdStrike to go beyond generic attack scenarios to emulate how adversaries could exploit interconnected weaknesses in a customer's environment to gain access to critical systems.

Powered by CrowdStrike SafeMind: SafeMind provides the purpose-built AI models and offensive harnesses that drive Agentic Adversary Emulation. Combining CrowdStrike’s latest adversary intelligence with deep visibility into customer environments, these systems emulate real-world adversary behavior at machine speed, continuously exploring attack paths and adapting as new weaknesses are discovered. Operating within customer-approved boundaries, they identify exploitable weaknesses, reveal how attackers could chain them together, and demonstrate what adversaries could achieve against critical assets.

During early access, CrowdStrike will work closely with selected customers to conduct controlled red teaming within defined safeguards and customer-approved boundaries, while refining the operational guardrails for safe execution in production environments.

Bringing Threat Intelligence to Smartphones

As AI accelerates adversary operations, security teams need trusted intelligence to make faster decisions, wherever they are. CrowdStrike is bringing its industry-leading threat intelligence and agentic AI capabilities to a new mobile app for iOS and Android. Available to CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary Intelligence Premium customers, the app extends the Falcon experience beyond the desktop, providing direct access to the latest intelligence reports and the Threat Intelligence Agent.

Through the new app, customers can:

Stay ahead of emerging threats: Access expert-validated intelligence on adversaries, including their latest activities, evolving tactics, and emerging campaigns, to understand threats as they develop.

Act faster: Ask the Threat Intelligence Agent questions in natural language to quickly understand adversaries, campaigns, vulnerabilities, and emerging threats, identify what matters most, and determine what actions to take.

Make informed decisions anywhere: Access trusted intelligence and AI-driven analysis wherever decisions need to be made, without being tied to a desktop or the Falcon console.

Advancing Adversary-Driven Security for the AI Era

With Agentic Adversary Emulation and the new threat intelligence mobile app, CrowdStrike is expanding how organizations put adversary intelligence to work, from proactively simulating attacks and strengthening defenses to making informed security decisions wherever they are. Title: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On
Context: New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection
Full Text:
AI is accelerating both sides of cloud security. Developers and coding agents are writing more code, pulling in more open source packages, and launching more cloud and AI workloads than security teams can review by hand. Adversaries use AI to move faster, and they are targeting everything organizations build and run, from the packages in automated pipelines, to the identities that control cloud resources, to the infrastructure powering AI applications.

Security teams must keep pace on both fronts to defend against this acceleration and secure the cloud their AI runs on. CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security is built for this. It is powered by adversary intelligence tracking 290+ adversaries, so detections and risk prioritization reflect how attackers operate in the cloud. It runs on the same CrowdStrike Falcon platform that connects endpoint and identity protection with SOC operations, extending protection from developer endpoints and software supply chains to cloud workloads. Because proactive security and real-time cloud detection and response (CDR) share one platform, the exposure and attack path context teams build before an attack becomes the context analysts use to stop one.

The latest Falcon Cloud Security innovations, all now generally available, put this advantage to work from build to runtime. They help organizations stop compromised software before production, protect AI workloads and the infrastructure supporting them, and detect cloud attacks in seconds. Proactive security informs runtime defense by giving teams the context to understand risks and when to act on them. This connected defense spans business and mission-critical environments, including some of the hardest to secure.

Reduce Risk and Stop Threats Before Production

Securing the cloud that AI runs on starts with understanding where organizations are exposed and whether software entering production can be trusted. Falcon Cloud Security connects cloud risk, application context, and adversary intelligence to help teams close exposures before software is deployed.

Stop Supply Chain Threats

AI coding agents are pulling open source packages into automated builds faster than teams can review them. Adversaries can exploit that trust by compromising otherwise legitimate software. CrowdStrike observed ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day.1 A compromised dependency does not need a CVE to be dangerous, which means vulnerability scanning alone can miss the threat.

Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends the adversary intelligence CrowdStrike uses to detect and quarantine malicious packages on endpoints into container images. Falcon Cloud Security identifies compromised npm and PyPI packages during CI/CD and registry scanning, automatically reassesses previously scanned images as new threats are confirmed, and identifies affected running containers.

At deployment, the Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller uses image assessment policies to alert on or block compromised images before they reach production. Together, endpoint and cloud protection connect the defense from package download through deployment to help teams stop compromised software.

Expand Cloud Risk and Asset Visibility

Security teams need to understand how exposures combine into opportunities for an adversary. Cloud Risks coverage in Falcon Cloud Security now extends to Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, where it connects exposure, effective permissions, vulnerabilities, and sensitive data context to identify high-risk combinations that isolated assessments can miss.

Supporting coverage expansions help teams assess more of their environment. Agentless Vulnerability Scanning for Google Cloud adds vulnerability and malware discovery for Linux-based Google Compute Engine instances without requiring additional sensor deployment. Expanded OCI inventory brings additional infrastructure, identities, and secrets into view. Together, these updates help teams account for more cloud assets and assess workloads where they cannot install an additional sensor.

Understand Applications and What Exposes Them

Cloud risk becomes more actionable when teams can connect it to the applications their business depends on. Expanded Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) brings containerized applications into Application Explorer with workload and cloud context, allowing Cloud Risks to evaluate them alongside other resources. Teams can identify combinations such as an internet-exposed Kubernetes workload running code with a remote code execution vulnerability.

New package exports map vulnerable dependencies to their associated applications, which helps teams assess blast radius and plan remediation across the application fleet. Enhanced third-party API integration findings identify external payment-service integrations and the operations applications invoke, helping teams assess exposure when a provider is compromised and uncover unauthorized integrations. The result is a clearer picture of which applications are affected and where remediation is needed.

Stop Cloud Attacks and Protect AI Workloads at Runtime

When an adversary gains access, security teams need to recognize malicious behavior, understand what is at risk, and respond while the attack is in progress. Falcon Cloud Security connects real-time detection with workload, identity, and exposure context to help defenders interrupt attacks across cloud environments.

Connect Cloud Exposure with Real-Time Detection and Response

CrowdStrike is extending Real-Time CDR to Microsoft Azure and Kubernetes, building on existing coverage for AWS and Google Cloud. Falcon Cloud Security continuously analyzes cloud audit activity as it streams, applies adversary-informed detection logic, and surfaces high-fidelity detections in seconds. Identity, asset, workload, endpoint, and adversary context helps analysts investigate and act while the attack is still in progress. All within the Falcon console, they can deny credentials or shut down compromised instances, or automate those actions with CrowdStrike® Charlotte Agentic SOAR to contain the intrusion before it spreads.

New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection. Suspicious behavior is evaluated alongside conditions such as dormant identities, elevated privileges, public exposure, and sensitive data so analysts can understand its potential consequences and prioritize response. A privileged action from a long-inactive identity, for example, takes on different significance when viewed alongside the conditions that could make it dangerous.

AI-based Anomaly Detection strengthens this defense by identifying suspicious behavior that predefined rules may miss. A dedicated machine learning model learns each customer’s baseline and evaluates deviations involving identities, APIs, and resources across multiple events to help uncover threats such as account takeover and API misuse. It is now available for AWS CloudTrail.

Together, these innovations connect attack behavior with exposure to help teams identify affected identities and workloads, assess potential impact, and focus response.

Protect AI Workloads and the Cloud They Run On

Securing AI requires protection for both AI interactions and the environments supporting them. Falcon Container Sensor and Falcon Guardian support for Anthropic APIs extends runtime detection to the prompt layer for supported AI workloads to help teams identify threats in AI interactions while maintaining a unified view of their environment.

Workload protection for Google Cloud Workstations brings cloud development environments into Falcon Cloud Security visibility, detection, and response workflows. Expanded AWS Bedrock AgentCore inventory complements that protection with visibility into the managed infrastructure supporting AI applications. These capabilities address distinct needs: detecting threats in supported AI interactions, protecting development workloads, and accounting for the resources behind AI applications.

Extend Protection to Regulated and Specialized Environments

Government agencies and regulated enterprises need cloud protection that reaches the environments their missions depend on. Expanded Falcon Cloud Security capabilities in US-GOV-1 and US-GOV-2 bring cloud detections, detection-rule management, and CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM workflows to GovCloud, including Kubernetes audit-log detections across Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google GKE. Amazon S3 scanning in Merlin also extends sensitive-data discovery to customers in that environment.

DaemonSet support for Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Z and IBM LinuxONE, along with DaemonSet sensor support for Ubuntu Kairos, extends workload protection to specialized infrastructure. Teams can bring more of their environment into Falcon platform protection workflows without introducing separate tools, consoles, and investigation processes for each workload type. This helps close coverage gaps while reducing operational overhead.

Cloud Defense Built Around How Attacks Unfold

Securing the cloud AI runs on means understanding the software entering a build, the identities accessing cloud services, the data applications handle, and the behavior of workloads in production. Adversaries do not separate the software supply chain from the cloud identities, workloads, and data they want to reach, and defenders cannot either.

Falcon Cloud Security is built for this reality, combining CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence with endpoint, identity, and cloud context to unite proactive security and real-time detection and response on one platform. That connection matters at every critical decision: whether to allow software into production, which exposures to fix first, and how to contain an attack already underway. Proactive context makes every real-time detection more precise and every response faster.

Expanded protection for government clouds and specialized infrastructure brings more of that connected defense to government agencies and regulated enterprises, helping protect the environments their businesses and missions depend on.

Title: CrowdStrike Brings Enterprise Browser Security to the Falcon Platform
Context: The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface
Full Text:
The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface. Employees rely on the browser to access business applications, interact with AI tools, and handle sensitive data. Knowing this, attackers seek to exploit browser sessions for credential theft and data exfiltration.

Today, CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser is natively available on the CrowdStrike Falcon platform, extending protection into the browser. Security teams can manage browser security alongside existing Falcon capabilities through a unified platform experience. This provides a simpler way to protect browser activity across managed and unmanaged devices, without requiring employees to adopt a dedicated enterprise browser or reroute traffic.

The availability of Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser on the Falcon platform delivers three key advantages:

Less to manage: Browser security, secure remote access, and BYOD/contractor access are managed directly within the organization’s Falcon platform environment.

Faster to deploy: Protection works in the browsers teams already use; there is no need to deploy a dedicated browser or reroute traffic.

Coverage where the sensor can't go: Protection extends to unmanaged, BYOD, and contractor devices without mobile device management (MDM) enrollment.

Stop Browser-Based Threats, Protect Data, and Secure Access

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser provides real-time security controls inside browser sessions, where users access applications, handle sensitive data, and interact with AI tools. Its browser-layer capabilities address five important use cases:

Blocking browser-based attacks: Runtime inspection helps detect and disrupt malicious browser activity, including phishing, ClickFix, malicious scripts, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

Identity and session protection: Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser extends protection beyond authentication to help stop session token theft and session hijacking within active browser sessions.

Data and AI controls at the point of use: Teams can enforce policies on browser actions such as copy, paste, upload, and download; this helps prevent sensitive data from reaching unsanctioned web applications and generative AI tools.

Browser extension management: Security teams can inventory browser extensions, evaluate their risk, and enforce policies that allow or block risky extensions across supported browsers.

Secure access to private applications: Policy-controlled access to internal web applications and resources is provided for employees and contractors, including on unmanaged devices, without relying on traditional VPN or VDI for supported workflows.

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser complements the broader security context of the Falcon platform. With browser telemetry available in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, analysts can search, investigate, and correlate browser activity with endpoint, identity, and third-party data to accelerate triage and response. With richer context and more places to act, security teams can follow the adversary rather than the boundaries between products.

Built for How Teams Work

As enterprise work increasingly happens in browsers, SaaS applications, and AI tools, browser security can no longer operate in isolation. By bringing Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser into the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike extends protection into the browser while unifying security operations across more of the enterprise attack surface. This helps organizations stop threats, protect sensitive data, and reduce operational complexity.

Full Text:
AI agents are transforming enterprise computing. What began with employees using AI assistants is evolving into autonomous agents that access enterprise resources, invoke tools, execute code, and take action at machine speed.

This introduces a new security and safety challenge. Organizations must protect agents from attacks while ensuring those agents operate safely and as intended. Security teams need to discover where agents operate, understand what they were instructed to do, trace their actions, and intervene when their behavior becomes dangerous.

Traditional security approaches provide only part of the picture. Endpoint runtime security monitors execution but lacks the AI-specific context needed to explain what triggered it. Network inspection can monitor AI communications but not the actions that agents take on systems. Agent-level integrations can inspect AI interactions but cannot reveal downstream execution.

At Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike unveiled innovations that advance AI detection and response (AIDR) across three critical dimensions: architecture, coverage, and controls. We also introduced a new AI kill switch for CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian that empowers security teams to rapidly cut off AI model access at AI gateways when agents become dangerous. And we shared the general availability of CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Guardian, which extends 24/7 managed detection and response to AI security.

The Right Architecture for Securing AI Agents

Securing AI agents requires visibility and control across three critical layers: OS-level runtime execution, network communications, and agent interactions. Falcon Guardian brings these layers together to connect what agents are instructed to do with what they execute.

OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they run, and resources they access. This visibility is not achievable directly via network inspection or per-agent hook integration approaches.

Endpoint network inspection extends visibility into agent communications (Pre-beta): CrowdStrike announced plans to expand this capability to macOS, where it will inspect traffic entering and leaving the endpoint to help security teams identify risky interactions.

Agent-level hooks provide direct inspection and policy enforcement within supported AI agents (Available now): Hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor enable organizations to inspect prompts and block malicious activity at the source, before harmful actions are executed.

Together, these three layers give Falcon Guardian visibility into agent instructions, communications, and runtime execution. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects this activity, linking what agents were instructed to do with what they actually executed and the resources they affected. This gives security teams the context to understand agent behavior, investigate threats, and trace their impact from prompt to process.

See it in action:

The Right Coverage: Secured AI Wherever It Operates

Falcon Guardian initially focused on securing workforce AI adoption and autonomous agents at the endpoint, where employees interact with AI and agents execute with user permissions.

Now, as enterprises build and deploy their own agents in production environments, CrowdStrike is expanding Falcon Guardian's AI-specific protections across more of the cloud infrastructure the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform already secures. Newly announced capabilities will extend Falcon Guardian coverage across Linux, cloud workloads, Kubernetes, and managed AI platforms.

Expanded cloud coverage (Pre-beta): On Linux, Falcon Guardian will bring agent discovery, visibility, and AI-specific detections to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. In cloud workloads and Kubernetes, Falcon Guardian will extend these capabilities to enterprise-developed AI agents and applications, including those built with LangChain and LangGraph. Using the Falcon Linux sensor, deployed directly or as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, Falcon Guardian will connect AI activity with surrounding runtime, workload, and identity context.

For provider-managed AI environments, Falcon Guardian will expand agent discovery and AI-layer visibility, beginning with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This will help security teams identify managed agents, understand their components and interactions, and assess AI-specific risks without requiring access to provider-controlled infrastructure.

Title: CrowdStrike to Acquire Fiddler to Deliver Falcon Observe for AI Agent Observability
Context: It will become part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform as CrowdStrike Falcon® Observe, generally available in Q4 FY27
Full Text:
I am delighted to announce CrowdStrike’s intent to acquire Fiddler at Fal.Con EU 2026. Fiddler, a leader in AI observability, will help ensure enterprise AI agents act as intended with pre-deployment evaluation and continuous behavioral monitoring as part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform.

Every business deploying AI agents asks the same questions: What are our agents doing? Are they staying on task? Are they acting in a way that could put the business at risk?

AI agents don’t have to be compromised to be dangerous. Those that stay within their guardrails can make a bad decision or take harmful action using valid credentials and approved enterprise tools. Businesses must be able to trace agents’ activity and explain anomalies as these concerns become top of mind among auditors, regulators, board members, and risk managers.

Enterprise AI safety requires a comprehensive approach: Evaluate agents before deployment, understand their decisions and actions, and continuously monitor their behavior. AI observability provides a lens into agent behavior before and after they ship. AI explainability shows why agents made their decisions and where their actions may have gone awry.

Fiddler delivers both. It will become part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform as CrowdStrike Falcon® Observe, generally available in Q4 FY27. With this acquisition, CrowdStrike will extend our AI security capabilities beyond protecting AI systems into proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day.

Building AI Trust in the Agentic Enterprise

Unlike traditional software, AI agents can make autonomous decisions, invoke tools, and take actions across enterprise systems. If software can act autonomously, security needs a record of those actions: what each agent decided, how it acted, what it changed, and the tools it used. They must know whether the agent made the correct decisions to follow its intended task.

As an example: Consider an AI agent using approved tools and valid credentials to process a customer refund. The agent makes an incorrect decision and approves a refund that violates company policy. Traditional security controls may see legitimate activity, but AI explainability reveals why the agent made that decision and where its behavior went wrong.

Fiddler provides AI observability for the agentic era. It helps organizations identify misaligned agents before they are deployed and continues to monitor agent behavior post-deployment so businesses have full visibility into what they’re doing and why.

Before deployment, teams can compare prompts, models, and configurations to evaluate whether agents perform intended tasks safely and accurately before they reach production.

After deployment, teams can trace agents’ decisions and reasoning paths across the full agent hierarchy to detect issues like behavioral drift and unintended actions before they cause harm. Fiddler reconstructs the agent’s decision-making process so teams can trace each failure to the step that caused it.

Fiddler supports auditable AI governance across organizations’ existing agents and tools. Its granular view of agents’ decision-making covers first-party and third-party agents across the enterprise so teams have the data they need to support compliance and audits. Businesses also gain explainability across the frameworks they run, as Fiddler enables teams to instrument agents through OpenTelemetry and supports LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands, and Google ADK.

As part of the Falcon platform, Fiddler will connect AI agent intent and behavior with Falcon security telemetry across endpoints, identity, cloud, and runtime environments. This will help security teams understand why an agent took an action and what happened across the enterprise as a result. By connecting agent decisions with enterprise security context, CrowdStrike will provide visibility that goes beyond standalone AI observability.

CrowdStrike Delivers the Enterprise AI Control Plane

This milestone extends CrowdStrike’s leadership in protecting the agentic enterprise. Our acquisition of Fiddler, together with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian innovations announced today, will bring comprehensive AI security and safety solutions to the Falcon platform.

CrowdStrike can already establish AI agents as trusted identities, connect those identities to the humans operating them, grant access to business systems based on real-time risk, and secure AI agents at runtime. Fiddler will extend the Falcon platform to the earliest stages of the agent lifecycle, before deployment, to monitor their behavior before and after production, and explain the decisions they make.

Falcon Guardian protects AI agents from attacks and misuse. Falcon Observe evaluates and explains whether agents behave as intended. Together, they secure AI operations in the agentic enterprise.

Title: Introducing AI Kill Switch: Taking Control When AI Agents Go Rogue
Context: The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches
Full Text:
One Kill Switch with Comprehensive Enforcement Points

Coming soon, CrowdStrike will extend AI Kill Switch beyond gateway enforcement to deliver coordinated agent containment across the Falcon platform.

AI agents operate across endpoints, cloud environments, SaaS applications, browsers, and enterprise identities, often spanning multiple environments in a single chain of activity. When an agent goes rogue, stopping it shouldn't require security teams to investigate and respond separately in every environment.

CrowdStrike's vision is one AI Kill Switch coordinating response across multiple enforcement points. This will bring together the security capabilities of the Falcon platform and its broader ecosystem to contain rogue agents wherever they operate, including:

Endpoint agents: Terminate rogue agents and associated processes directly on affected endpoints and prevent them from restarting.

Cloud agents: Contain or terminate compromised agents operating in cloud environments.

User and agent identities: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen Identity Security to revoke agent permissions at runtime and restrict access to enterprise resources.

SaaS agents: Extend containment through CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield to restrict or terminate agent activity within SaaS environments.

Browser sessions: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser to terminate sessions and disrupt unauthorized activity through web applications.

This evolution will enable increasingly targeted containment so security teams can stop individual rogue agents or groups of agents with surgical precision while minimizing disruption to business operations.

CrowdStrike's architectural advantage goes beyond individual enforcement mechanisms. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects AI intent to downstream execution, revealing what an agent was asked to do, what it did, and which systems or resources were affected. This context helps security teams understand the threat and determine where to intervene. CrowdStrike Charlotte Agentic SOAR provides the no-code security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) capabilities to coordinate enforcement across the Falcon platform, enabling automated AI Kill Switch workflows triggered by AI-specific detections or risky agent behavior.

Rather than responding to isolated events through disconnected tools, security teams will be able to coordinate containment across the agentic attack surface.

Secure AI Adoption Without Losing Control

AI agents are becoming a powerful part of enterprise operations. As their autonomy and reach expand, organizations need security that can keep pace.

With AI Kill Switch, CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges. This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.

The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches.
